description: A Single Mathematics B-style paper covering polar motion, ODEs, Fourier series, coordinate transforms, critical points, vector identities, and probability distributions.
instructions: Show sufficient working to justify each answer.
Answers should be exact unless a numerical approximation is requested.
Begin each main question on a new page when working on paper.
label: Paper 1

questions.stem: A particle moves in the plane with polar coordinates \(\theta=t\) and \(r=2\sec\theta\), for \(-\pi/2<t<\pi/2\).
questions.title: Polar Motion

parts.label: (a)
parts.prompt: Find the Cartesian equation of the trajectory and describe its sketch.
parts.answer: Using \(x=r\cos\theta\) and \(y=r\sin\theta\), we get \(x=2\sec\theta\cos\theta=2\). Also \(y=2\sec\theta\sin\theta=2\tan t\). Hence the particle moves on the vertical line \(x=2\). As \(t\) increases from \(-\pi/2\) to \(\pi/2\), \(y=2\tan t\) increases from \(-\infty\) to \(\infty\), so the sketch is the whole vertical line traversed upward.

parts.label: (b)
parts.prompt: Compute the velocity and acceleration in Cartesian components.
parts.answer: The Cartesian position is \(\mathbf r(t)=(2,2\tan t)\). Differentiating gives the velocity \[\mathbf v(t)=(0,2\sec^2t).\] Differentiating once more gives the acceleration \[\mathbf a(t)=(0,4\sec^2t\tan t).\] The horizontal component of both velocity and acceleration is zero, as expected for motion along a vertical line.

parts.label: (c)
parts.prompt: If the particle has constant mass \(m\), express the force in terms of the Cartesian coordinate \(y\).
parts.answer: Since \(y=2\tan t\), we have \(\tan t=y/2\) and \(\sec^2t=1+\tan^2t=1+y^2/4\). The acceleration is vertical with component \[4\sec^2t\tan t=4\left(1+\frac{y^2}{4}\right)\frac{y}{2}=2y+\frac{y^3}{2}.\] Therefore \[\mathbf F=m\mathbf a=\left(0,m\left(2y+\frac{y^3}{2}\right)\right).\] This is a nonlinear vertical force depending only on displacement along the line.

parts.label: (a)
parts.prompt: Solve \(x''+2x'+x=e^{-t}\), subject to \(x(0)=0\) and \(x'(0)=1\).
parts.answer: The operator is \((D+1)^2\). Put \(x=e^{-t}u(t)\). Then \((D+1)^2x=e^{-t}u''\), so the equation becomes \(u''=1\). Hence \(u=t^2/2+C_1t+C_0\), and \[x=e^{-t}\left(\frac{t^2}{2}+C_1t+C_0\right).\] The condition \(x(0)=0\) gives \(C_0=0\). Since \(x'=e^{-t}(u'-u)\), the condition \(x'(0)=1\) gives \(C_1=1\). Thus \[x(t)=e^{-t}\left(t+\frac{t^2}{2}\right).\]

parts.label: (b)
parts.prompt: Solve the Bernoulli equation \(\frac{dy}{dx}+y=xy^2\), subject to \(y(0)=1\).
parts.answer: Let \(z=y^{-1}\). Then \(z'=-y^{-2}y'\). From the equation, \(y'=xy^2-y\), so \[z'=-(x-y^{-1})=-x+z.\] Hence \(z'-z=-x\). The integrating factor is \(e^{-x}\), giving \[(ze^{-x})'=-xe^{-x}.\] Integrating, \(ze^{-x}=(x+1)e^{-x}+C\), so \(z=x+1+Ce^x\). Since \(y(0)=1\), \(z(0)=1\), hence \(C=0\). Therefore \[y(x)=\frac{1}{x+1}.\]

questions.stem: Let \(g(x)=x\) on \((-\pi,\pi]\), extended periodically with period \(2\pi\).
questions.title: Fourier Series of an Odd Function

parts.label: (a)
parts.prompt: Find the Fourier series of \(g\).
parts.answer: The function is odd, so \(a_0=a_n=0\). The sine coefficients are \[b_n=\frac{2}{\pi}\int_0^{\pi}x\sin nx\,dx.\] Integrating by parts with \(u=x\) and \(dv=\sin nx\,dx\), \[\int_0^{\pi}x\sin nx\,dx=\left[-\frac{x\cos nx}{n}\right]_0^{\pi}+\frac{1}{n}\int_0^{\pi}\cos nx\,dx=-\frac{\pi(-1)^n}{n}.\] Thus \(b_n=2(-1)^{n+1}/n\), and \[x\sim2\left(\sin x-\frac{\sin2x}{2}+\frac{\sin3x}{3}-\frac{\sin4x}{4}+\cdots\right).\]

parts.label: (b)
parts.prompt: Use Parseval's theorem to prove that \(\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\frac{1}{n^2}=\frac{\pi^2}{6}\).
parts.answer: Parseval's theorem gives \[\frac{1}{\pi}\int_{-\pi}^{\pi}x^2\,dx=\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}b_n^2.\] The left side is \[\frac{2}{\pi}\int_0^{\pi}x^2\,dx=\frac{2\pi^2}{3}.\] Since \(b_n=2(-1)^{n+1}/n\), the right side is \[\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\frac{4}{n^2}=4\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\frac{1}{n^2}.\] Therefore \[\frac{2\pi^2}{3}=4\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\frac{1}{n^2},\] and so \(\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}1/n^2=\pi^2/6\).

parts.label: (a)
parts.prompt: Show that \(\frac{\partial r}{\partial x}=\cos\theta\), \(\frac{\partial r}{\partial y}=\sin\theta\), \(\frac{\partial\theta}{\partial x}=-\frac{\sin\theta}{r}\), and \(\frac{\partial\theta}{\partial y}=\frac{\cos\theta}{r}\).
parts.answer: Since \(r=(x^2+y^2)^{1/2}\), \(r_x=x/r=\cos\theta\) and \(r_y=y/r=\sin\theta\). Also \(\theta=\tan^{-1}(y/x)\). Differentiating gives \[\theta_x=\frac{1}{1+(y/x)^2}\left(-\frac{y}{x^2}\right)=-\frac{y}{x^2+y^2}=-\frac{\sin\theta}{r},\] and \[\theta_y=\frac{1}{1+(y/x)^2}\frac{1}{x}=\frac{x}{x^2+y^2}=\frac{\cos\theta}{r}.\]

parts.label: (b)
parts.prompt: If \(F(r,\theta)=e^{r^2\cos2\theta}\), find \(F_\theta\).
parts.answer: Treat \(r\) as constant when differentiating with respect to \(\theta\). Since \(\frac{d}{d\theta}(r^2\cos2\theta)=-2r^2\sin2\theta\), the chain rule gives \[F_\theta=-2r^2\sin2\theta\,e^{r^2\cos2\theta}.\] This is the angular rate of change of the transformed scalar field at fixed radius.

parts.label: (c)
parts.prompt: Evaluate \(\iint_R(1+x^2+y^2)\,dA\), where \(R\) is the quarter-disc \(0\le r\le2\), \(0\le\theta\le\pi/2\).
parts.answer: In polar coordinates, \(x^2+y^2=r^2\) and \(dA=r\,dr\,d\theta\). Therefore \[\iint_R(1+x^2+y^2)\,dA=\int_0^{\pi/2}\int_0^2(1+r^2)r\,dr\,d\theta.\] The radial integral is \[\int_0^2(r+r^3)\,dr=\left[\frac{r^2}{2}+\frac{r^4}{4}\right]_0^2=2+4=6.\] Multiplying by \(\pi/2\), the value is \(3\pi\).

questions.section: Section E: Critical Points and Vector Calculus
questions.title: Critical Points with a Parameter

parts.label: (a)
parts.prompt: Find and classify the critical point when \(b=5\).
parts.answer: The first derivatives are \(f_x=2x-4y\) and \(f_y=2by-4x\). When \(b=5\), the equations are \(2x-4y=0\) and \(10y-4x=0\). The first gives \(x=2y\), and substituting into the second gives \(10y-8y=0\), so \(y=0\) and \(x=0\). The Hessian is \[H=\begin{pmatrix}2&-4\\-4&10\end{pmatrix},\] with determinant \(20-16=4>0\) and \(f_{xx}=2>0\). Thus \((0,0)\) is a local minimum.

parts.label: (b)
parts.prompt: Find the critical set when \(b=4\), and explain why the usual Hessian test is inconclusive.
parts.answer: When \(b=4\), the equations are \(2x-4y=0\) and \(8y-4x=0\). Both are equivalent to \(x=2y\), so every point on the line \(x=2y\) is critical. The Hessian is \[H=\begin{pmatrix}2&-4\\-4&8\end{pmatrix},\] whose determinant is \(16-16=0\). Since the determinant is zero, the second-derivative criterion is inconclusive.

parts.label: (c)
parts.prompt: Describe the surface when \(b=4\).
parts.answer: For \(b=4\), \[f(x,y)=x^2+4y^2-4xy=(x-2y)^2.\] Hence \(f\ge0\), and \(f=0\) exactly on the line \(x=2y\). The critical set is therefore a flat valley of global minima rather than an isolated critical point.

questions.section: Section F: Multiple Integrals and Vector Identities
questions.title: Divergence, Curl, and Identities

parts.label: (a)
parts.prompt: Describe the vector field in the plane \(z=0\).
parts.answer: In the plane \(z=0\), the field is \(\mathbf V=(-y/2,x/2,0)\). At each point the vector is perpendicular to the radial vector \((x,y,0)\), since \((-y/2,x/2,0)\cdot(x,y,0)=0\). Its magnitude is \(\frac12\sqrt{x^2+y^2}\), so the field represents anticlockwise rotation about the \(z\)-axis, growing linearly with distance from the origin.

parts.label: (b)
parts.prompt: Compute \(\nabla\cdot\mathbf V\) and \(\nabla\times\mathbf V\).
parts.answer: The divergence is \[\nabla\cdot\mathbf V=\frac{\partial}{\partial x}\left(-\frac y2\right)+\frac{\partial}{\partial y}\left(\frac x2\right)+\frac{\partial}{\partial z}(z^2)=2z.\] For the curl, \[\nabla\times\mathbf V=(0-0,0-0,\partial_x(x/2)-\partial_y(-y/2))=(0,0,1).\] The curl confirms a constant positive rotational tendency about the \(z\)-axis.

parts.label: (c)
parts.prompt: Show that \(\nabla\times(\nabla f)=\mathbf0\) for a smooth scalar function \(f(x,y,z)\).

questions.stem: A research visit uses three minibuses and a continuous model for equipment weights.
questions.title: Counting and Continuous Distributions

parts.label: (a)
parts.prompt: Twelve labelled students are assigned to minibuses with \(3\), \(4\), and \(5\) seats. How many assignments fill all seats?
parts.answer: Choose the \(3\) students for the first bus, then the \(4\) students for the second, and the remaining \(5\) go on the third. The number of assignments is \[\binom{12}{3}\binom{9}{4}=\frac{12!}{3!4!5!}.\] The buses have different capacities, so the bus labels matter and no additional division is needed.

parts.label: (b)
parts.prompt: Four of the students are physicists. If all assignments are equally likely, find the probability that all four physicists are on the largest bus.
parts.answer: The largest bus has \(5\) seats. If all four physicists are on it, choose its remaining passenger from the \(8\) non-physicists, then distribute the remaining \(7\) students between the buses of sizes \(3\) and \(4\). The favourable count is \(8\cdot\frac{7!}{3!4!}\). Dividing by the total \(\frac{12!}{3!4!5!}\), the probability is \[\frac{8\cdot7!/(3!4!)}{12!/(3!4!5!)}=\frac{8\cdot5!7!}{12!}.\]

parts.label: (c)
parts.prompt: A positive random variable has density \(f_X(x)=\alpha x^{-3}\) for \(x\ge1\), and \(0\) otherwise. Find \(\alpha\) and \(E[X]\).
parts.answer: For a valid density, \[1=\int_1^{\infty}\alpha x^{-3}\,dx=\alpha\left[-\frac{1}{2x^2}\right]_1^{\infty}=\frac{\alpha}{2}.\] Hence \(\alpha=2\). The expectation is \[E[X]=\int_1^{\infty}x\cdot2x^{-3}\,dx=2\int_1^{\infty}x^{-2}\,dx=2.\] Thus the density has finite mean equal to \(2\).

parts.label: (d)
parts.prompt: Find the cumulative distribution function and the probability \(P(X>3)\).
parts.answer: For \(x<1\), \(F_X(x)=0\). For \(x\ge1\), \[F_X(x)=\int_1^x2t^{-3}\,dt=\left[-t^{-2}\right]_1^x=1-\frac{1}{x^2}.\] Therefore \[F_X(x)=\begin{cases}0,&x<1,\\1-x^{-2},&x\ge1.\end{cases}\] The tail probability is \[P(X>3)=1-F_X(3)=\frac{1}{9}.\]
